text: Bridges; edge-biconnected components and their tree.

A bridge (桥 , 割边) is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph: here 3–4 and 5–7 (dashed). Tarjan's idea: DFS gives each node a time dfn[u]; low[u] is the smallest dfn reachable from u's subtree using at most one non-tree edge.
Tree edge u → v is a bridge exactly when low[v] > dfn[u]: nothing in v's subtree can climb back to u or above without that edge. One DFS, O(n + m).
Edge (u, v) seen from u Update tree edge: v not visited yet dfs(v), then low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]) back edge: v already visited (not the edge we came in on) low[u] = min(low[u], dfn[v])
Skip the edge id you came in on, not the parent node: with two parallel edges u–v, the second one is a real way back, and 3–4 doubled is not a bridge. P1656 炸铁路 lists the bridges sorted.
Start the DFS from every unvisited node: the graph may be disconnected. Recursion depth can reach n; enlarge the stack or write it iteratively for n ≈ 10⁶.

Remove all bridges: what stays connected are the edge-biconnected components (边双连通分量): inside one, any two nodes have two edge-disjoint paths. Shrinking each component to a point turns the graph into a tree whose edges are the bridges.

To make the whole graph bridge-free, join leaves of that tree in pairs: ⌈leaves / 2⌉ new edges (P2860). Here the tree is {1,2,3} – {4,5,6} – {7}: two leaves, one new road. "Most bosses on one path" (CF1000E) is the diameter of the same tree.
Cut vertices; blocks; the block-cut tree.
A cut vertex (割点) is a node whose removal disconnects the graph: here 3, 4 and 5. Same dfn / low. A non-root u is a cut vertex if some child v has low[v] ≥ dfn[u] (v's subtree cannot get above u).
The root is a cut vertex if it has two or more DFS children.
Compare with bridges: ≥ for nodes, > for edges. For cut vertices a back edge to u itself still leaves v's subtree stuck below u, so equality counts.
Using dfn[parent] in low is fine for cut vertices: low[v] = dfn[u] still passes the test low[v] ≥ dfn[u]. For bridges it is not fine, which is why bridges.cpp skips the incoming edge.
Counting the pairs cut apart when a node is removed (P3469 BLO): while scanning u, add sz[v]·(n − sz[v]) for each child v with low[v] ≥ dfn[u], plus the part above.

Vertex-biconnected components (点双连通分量 , blocks): maximal parts with no cut vertex of their own. A cut vertex belongs to several blocks (3 is in {1,2,3} and {3,4}). Keep a stack of nodes; when low[v] ≥ dfn[u], pop down to v, and the popped nodes plus u form a block.
Joining each block (a "square" node) to its members gives the block-cut tree (圆方树): any graph question about "nodes every path must pass" becomes a tree path question (P4630 铁人两项 , P4606,
Tarjan SCC, condensation DP, 2-SAT.
one SCC: weight 1+2+3 weights = node ids

In a directed graph, a strongly connected component (强连通分量 , SCC) is a maximal set where every node reaches every other. Tarjan again: keep a stack of visited nodes still waiting for a component; low[u] uses only edges to nodes still on the stack. When low[u] == dfn[u], u is the first node of its SCC: pop down to u.

Shrinking every SCC to one node (缩点) leaves a DAG. Tarjan numbers the SCCs in reverse topological order (a component is finished after everything it reaches), so a DP over the DAG can simply run from the largest SCC number down.

Largest node-weight path where nodes may repeat (P3387): inside an SCC you can collect everything, so the answer is the heaviest path in the DAG of SCCs: 6 + 4 + 5 = 15. "Cows loved by all" (P2341): exactly one SCC with out-degree 0 in the DAG, and its size is the answer. Fewest sources to reach everything (P1262):
SCCs with in-degree 0.
Use onStack, not just dfn: an edge into an SCC that is already finished must not lower low[u], otherwise two different components merge.

2-SAT: n boolean variables, each clause "xi = a or xj = b". Make two nodes per variable (true / false); a clause gives two implications "if not this, then that". It is unsatisfiable exactly when some x and ¬x are in the same SCC (P4782).

Choosing values: take for each variable the side whose SCC comes later in topological order, i.e. the smaller Tarjan number. Then no chosen node implies its own opposite. Problems with "choose one of two per item" plus pairwise conflicts are 2-SAT (P3825 游戏).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. dfn[u]: DFS time; low[u]: smallest dfn reachable from u's subtree with one back edge.
2. Bridge u → v: low[v] > dfn[u]. Skip the incoming edge id (parallel edges).
3. Cut vertex: non-root with a child low[v] ≥ dfn[u]; root with ≥ 2 DFS children.
4. Edge-BCCs: remove bridges; the components form a tree. Make bridge-free: ⌈leaves / 2⌉.
5. Vertex-BCCs: node stack; on low[v] ≥ dfn[u] pop to v, add u. Block-cut tree.
6. SCC: stack + onStack; low uses only nodes on the stack; root when low == dfn.
7. Tarjan SCC numbers = reverse topological order. Condense ⇒ DAG ⇒ DP.
8. 2-SAT: (a ∨ b) ⇒ ¬a → b, ¬b → a; impossible iff x, ¬x share an SCC; pick the smaller Tarjan number.
